nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Where does more than 70% of the global cocoa supply originate from?
nodes.answer: More than 70% of the global cocoa supply originates from the West African Cocoa belt, stretching from the coast of Sierra Leone to Cameroon.
nodes.paragraph: More than 70% of the global cocoa supply originates from the West African Cocoa belt, stretching from the coast of Sierra Leone to Cam- eroon (Wessel and Quist-Wessel 2015). However, cocoa is intertwined with environmental and eco- nomic challenges such as deforestation for agricul- tural purposes and persistent poverty (Sassen et al. 2022; Vliet et al. 2021). Simultaneously, the suitable range for cocoa production is expected to decrease due to challenges such as drought and hotter tempera- tures brought about by climate change (Ariza-Sala- manca et al. 2023; Schroth et al. 2016). As Nigeria S largest agricultural commodity, bringing in over 200 billion (~ $500 million USD) in 2021 (Nigeria Bureau of Statistics 2022), cocoa is an important contributor to the country S economy. However, climate change could impact Nigeria S ambitions to increase its cocoa output and diversify away from its heavy reliance on oil exports (Schroth et al. 2016; Awoyemi and Aderinoye-Abdulwahab 2019). Nigeria has already experienced an average temperature increase of 0.19 C per decade over the past 30 years (World Bank 2021) and continued cli- mate changes are expected to further challenge the country S development objectives (Okon et al.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why is changing population diets described as complex?
nodes.answer: Changing population diets is complex because it requires changes at several levels, including influencing consumer choices and behavior.
nodes.paragraph: BMC Medicine (2025) 23:150 Background Current levels of meat consumption in Western coun - tries exceed both dietary guidelines for human health as well as recommendations aimed at climate change miti - gation [1 3]. Especially processed meat consumption is associated with increased chronic disease risk, such as cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, and some forms of cancer [2 8]. Further, the production of specifically red and processed meat is considered to be an important contributor to the ongoing climate crisis as it contributes to biodiversity loss, reduced water quality, and global greenhouse gas emissions [3, 9]. Therefore, a shift from diets rich in predominantly animal-based to predomi - nantly plant-based protein is crucial for a sustainable future, enhancing both human and planetary health [1, 9]. Changing population diets is complex and requires changes at several levels. As supermarkets are a place where most consumers in Western societies buy their groceries and thus reach a wide range of individuals, this is a setting identified as promising place to shift con - sumer choices at population level.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the primary health benefits of Animal Source Foods (Asks) and who could benefit from increased consumption?
nodes.answer: Asks are rich in nutrients commonly lacking globally and can make significant contributions to healthy diets. Many populations in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia could benefit from increased consumption of Asks due to the nutrient density they provide.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How has the shift towards imported foods affected the health of Pacific Island countries?
nodes.answer: The dependence on imported foods has contributed to one of the highest prevalence rates of diabetes and obesity in the world due to a shift from locally grown and harvested food to lower nutritional quality imported food.
nodes.paragraph: 2021 ). Rural communities are in no way immune from imported food and changes in dietary preferences; yet, changes in rural food environments appear to be occurring more slowly due to the continued availability, low-cost, and often prefer - ence for local foods in the Solomon Islands (Pitman 2016 ). Furthermore, uneven experiences of food system change relate directly to gender, as rural women in the Solomon Islands conduct much of the household food provisioning, harvesting and cooking labor (Rabbitt et al. 2023 ). Post - colonial feminists highlight that gendered power relations are embedded within a wider context of (past and ongoing) colonialism (Mohanty 2003 ; Narayan and Harding 2000 ) with impacts on not only who conducts diverse food work, but how this work is recognized and valued (Hayes-Conroy and Hayes-Conroy 2013 ). Since colonialism, men in the Pacific have been recruited into the cash economy through plantation agriculture, shifting increasing power to men (Hermkens 2013 ; McKinnon et al. 2016 ). Simultaneously, indigenous food livelihoods were reconfigured through the influence of the cash economy and the Christian church, resulting in women S work and their traditional sources of power becoming devalued (Scheyvens 1998 ).
